gen1_finding_2026_09_08: THE LUA SCRIPT IS GEN1, CONFIRMED BYTE-FOR-BYTE. The ST LRi 2K listing is titled '15693 UID Changeable + Lua Script by Iceman Compatible ST LRi 2K (0-55 block)', and proxmark's client/luascripts/hf_15_magic.lua sends exactly four frames: 02213E00000000, 02213F69960000, 022138<uid hi>, 022139<uid lo>. 0x21 is ISO15693_WRITEBLOCK, so those are WRITE BLOCK at 0x3E, 0x3F, 0x38, 0x39 = blocks 62, 63, 56, 57 with 0, 0x6996 and the UID halves. That is the identical sequence SetTag15693Uid builds in armsrc/iso15693.c:3166, which is what `hf 15 csetuid` with no flag sends. Same frames, different transport -- client raw vs ARM helper. TWO CONSEQUENCES. (1) Our gen1 probe ALREADY covers the Lua method; there is no fourth mechanism to implement. (2) A product advertised as Lua-writable is a GEN1 product -- which is the card this PR has been blocked on for six rounds. #255's armed-gen1 hazard, the unlock/commit ordering inferred from proxmark's send order, and the post-wipe UID re-read are all untestable without one.
hypothesis_2026_09_08: The seller's 'pm3' mark correlates with presenting a GENUINE-looking identity. The four pm3-marked tags (three SLIX at IC ref 0x01, SLIX-S at 0x02) all carry NXP's manufacturer byte with an IC reference matching the part they claim, and proxmark identifies every one. Of the unmarked tags, four present something off: IC ref 0x21 on a SLIX that should read 0x01, unregistered manufacturer bytes 0x53 (silver pair) and 0x48 (gold). Reading: those are emulators carrying a programmed CFG, which is what produces an odd IC ref, while the pm3 tags are genuine NXP silicon made magic some other way. It cuts against the naive expectation, predicting that the tags proxmark CAN write look LEAST like magic. THIS IS A HYPOTHESIS and the write probe tests it. REVISED 2026-09-08: the keychain was originally counted as a fifth 'something off' on its IC ref 0x22. That was wrong -- it presents a fully coherent genuine ST identity, and it is a branded commercial product rather than part of the magic-card order at all. Excluding it as a freebie, the correlation covers four magic candidates against four pm3 tags, which is a cleaner claim than the one it replaces but rests on a smaller set. Do not treat 8 tags as 9 independent samples: the three SLIX share a UID prefix and the silver pair differ in two bytes, so this is more like four distinct products.

note: Expectations seeded from seller listings before any tag was read. Measurements are added by tools/iso15693_magic_probe.py; the expected block is never overwritten. Second order recorded 2026-09-08: 9 physical tags across 7 label types, seller-described as a mystery pack. The bag labels use `UID 0-NNB`, which decodes consistently across BOTH orders: `UID` is a claim that the UID is changeable, and `0-NN` is the writable block range, so 0-27B = 28 blocks, 0-63B = 64, 0-55B = 56. Cross-checked against measurement: our 28-block SLI tags, our 64-block TI cards, and the tool's own LRi2K-56 impersonation target all agree. order_context_2026_09_08: ORDERED 5, RECEIVED 9. The seller over-delivered as a favour after the purpose was explained, said he would substitute randomly, and MARKED the pm3-writable ones on the bag. So order lines do not map to delivered tags -- the bag labels are his own annotation of what each tag is and should be trusted over the order. The lines were: 1x 'Icode slix 1k 0-27b', 2x 'ST LRi 2K 0-55b', 1x '50X28mm', 1x '50x28mm slix 1k'. His words on the unmarked ones: 专用的读写设备, a DEDICATED READ/WRITE DEVICE -- hardware, not a script.
provenance_rule_2026_09_13: A magic card's UID, IC ref, DSFID, AFI and advertised geometry are all WRITABLE, so none of them identifies its silicon -- proxmark's TYPE line is a lookup on the UID's manufacturer byte, and the rest come from the CFG block. Treat every such field as a COSTUME unless the record says the read predates any write (original.pre_write). Found 2026-09-13 while adding gen-2-card, whose 'EM-Marin EM4237' identity turned out to be an expired access credential cloned onto it the day before the first instrumented read -- and had been cited as silicon in the PR. Two rules follow. Say what a card DID, not what it says it is. And when a card's identity came from somewhere else, record it under a name that says so: an inventory slot called `original` invites exactly the misreading that caused this.

SL2S5302.note: Hand-marked `pm3` by the seller, who said these are the ones proxmark can write. The unmarked ones he said need a custom application he did not supply -- so on an unmarked tag a negative result from our probe CONFIRMS his annotation and does not refute the UID claim. Physically marked SL2S5302 to tell it from slix-1k-50x28, the other 50x28mm white sticker. BLOCK COUNT UNKNOWN: the label states no range, and neither proxmark nor our app hardcodes SLI-S geometry -- both read it from GET SYSTEM INFO. Measure before assuming, because whether 56/57/62/63 exist decides if a gen1 attempt is destructive. || MEASURED 2026-09-08: SLIX-S, IC ref 0x02 as predicted from the decode table, and 40 BLOCKS x 4 -- a geometry this project had never measured, and one the label did not claim. 40 blocks means indices 0-39, so 56/57/62/63 are outside the DATA geometry. That does NOT make a gen1 attempt harmless, and this record said it did: blocks 56 and 57 accept a gen1 UID write on this card and the UID moves -- measured directly, see latch_2026_09_15. The UID registers are backdoor registers rather than memory, so they do not sit inside the advertised range and the block count says nothing about whether they exist. What 40 blocks does settle is the WIPE sweep, which never reaches them: 40 is below 49, so the absent run ends the sweep around block 47.

gen-2-card.note:
THE ORIGINAL GEN2 CARD, and the control the project's central write claim rests on. The 2026-08-17 regression five passed on it, and it was re-run as the control in the 2026-09-12 device session: it ACCEPTS unaddressed WRITE BLOCK, where white-coin and black-tag refuse it (#251). That behavioural contrast is measured and stands on its own.

WHAT THIS CARD IS, is unknown. It presents as EM-Marin EM4237 at IC ref 0x0F advertising 66 blocks because an expired access credential was cloned onto it on 2026-07-26 -- see `carries_cloned_credential`. Every field that names a chip is writable on a gen2 magic card: proxmark's TYPE is a lookup on the UID's manufacturer byte, and IC ref / block count / block size come from GET SYSTEM INFO, which is the CFG block. All of them were watched moving on this one card inside three hours on 2026-07-27 -- 105923: E0 16 3C.. / IC 0x0F / 66 blocks, gen2_write TRUE; 113213: the SAME UID at IC 0x8B / 64 blocks, after the gen2 csetuid stamped proxmark's default CFG; 120636: E0 07 C0 C1 C2 C3 C4 C5 (the synthetic tagit_64 test UID); 123035: E0 04 01 10 A1 A2 A3 A4 at 28 blocks (slix_28). The credential's identity says nothing about the card, and neither does any of the others.

What IS measured about the card: 64 physical blocks with a 2-block phantom tail above whatever it is currently advertising, gen2 magic, and that it accepts unaddressed WRITE BLOCK.

Consequence for anything citing it: the 'EM-Marin 0x0F vs TI Tag-it 0x8B' framing used in pr-round-10 reads as a silicon contrast and is not one. Both attributions are UID-manufacturer lookups on cards whose UIDs are writable, and 0x8B is also what THIS card reports after a plain gen2 CFG write. white-coin and black-tag are in a better position -- their TI presentation is the state they ARRIVED in rather than one we wrote -- but 'as shipped' is still not 'as fabricated'. Cite the BEHAVIOUR (accepts vs refuses unaddressed WRITE BLOCK), not the chip name.

armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.formatter_first_hardware_sighting: Incidental but worth having: 'Now reads: 00000000 00000000' is the Iso15693UidFormatGrouped output from the comment-cut delta's one code change, rendering correctly on hardware for the first time -- two 4-byte groups, 17 characters, inside the line budget.
armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.recovery: Recoverable, and the original UID is recorded here: hf 15 csetuid -u E002222450008303. gen1's frames are unaddressed (flags 0x02, no UID in the frame), so an invalid UID does not put the card out of reach.
armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.screen: UID changed / Wiped 58/58. The card's UID moved. Now reads: 00000000 00000000
armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.sweep_found_58_of_56_advertised: The wipe cleared 58 blocks against 56 advertised, with zero failures -- so blocks 56 and 57, the gen1 UID registers, were reached and zeroed. That is the sweep-above-advertised design working on gen1 silicon. It also demonstrates the rule it was built on: our own read-based capacity probe measured 56/56 on this card and UNDER-DETECTED BY TWO. Only a write settles whether a block exists, exactly as ISO15693_POLLER_WIPE_MAX_BLOCKS says -- which means the probe's capacity figure is a lower bound on any card whose high blocks accept writes without answering reads.
armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.what_it_settles: THE ARMED-GEN1 WIPE HAZARD IS REAL AND NOW DEMONSTRATED, not inferred. #255's central claim held: the wipe zeroed blocks 56/57, the armed card latched the result on power-up, and its identity moved. AND THE MITIGATION THIS PR SHIPS WORKED -- the post-power-cycle UID re-read caught it, uid_verified reached an answer, and the run reported uid_changed as Partial on the UID-changed screen rather than claiming a clean wipe. Six rounds argued this from proxmark's send order; it is now measured.
armed_gen1_wipe_2026_09_08.worse_than_documented: The UID did not move to another VALID identity -- it moved to ALL ZEROS. An ISO15693 UID must begin with 0xE0, so the card now answers with a non-conformant identity. #255 and the poller both describe this as the UID being 'moved' or 'changed', which understates it: the card is left without a valid UID at all. The screen printing 00000000 00000000 is honest and is the only route back, but a reader of either document would not expect zeros.

slix-1k-50mm.note: Hand-marked `pm3` by the seller, who said these are the ones proxmark can write. The unmarked ones he said need a custom application he did not supply -- so on an unmarked tag a negative result from our probe CONFIRMS his annotation and does not refute the UID claim. The bag labels use `UID 0-NNB`, which decodes consistently across BOTH orders: `UID` is a claim that the UID is changeable, and `0-NN` is the writable block range, so 0-27B = 28 blocks, 0-63B = 64, 0-55B = 56. Cross-checked against measurement: our 28-block SLI tags, our 64-block TI cards, and the tool's own LRi2K-56 impersonation target all agree. The FIRST order's plain tags were labelled '1024 bit' with NO UID claim and measured non-magic, so the notation distinguishes magic from plain rather than being decoration. || MEASURED 2026-09-08: SLIX, IC ref 0x01, advertises 28. ANOMALY: blocks 0 and 1 would not read -- 6 retries each in baseline and 6 more in capacity, so 12 consecutive failures -- while blocks 2-27 read fine. Capacity aborted entirely, since it needs block 0 as its anchor, so this tag has NO physical measurement. Marginal coupling is the obvious explanation (it is the only tag too large to sit flat on the HF pad) but it does not fit well: coupling drops reads at RANDOM, and this failed the same two addresses every time while its three siblings read all 28 blocks. Re-run it: if 0 and 1 fail again with the tag repositioned, that is a property of the tag rather than the placement. || 2026-09-08 RE-RUN TWICE MORE, 12 retries each, one contact-but-realigned and one with a ~20mm air gap: blocks 0 and 1 unreadable every time while 2-27 read fine. That is three sessions and 36+ attempts per block across three different couplings, so IT IS NOT COUPLING -- it is a property of the tag. The air gap did fix whatever was stopping the tag reading at all, which supports the over-coupling guess for the FIRST failure, but blocks 0/1 survived the fix. Still no physical measurement: capacity anchors on block 0. Hypothesis to test with the write probe -- if this is a magic tag, blocks 0/1 may be reserved or remapped by its magic implementation rather than faulty. || 2026-09-12 RESOLVED, AND IT WAS NEVER THE TAG. The 'unreadable' blocks 0/1 were a HARNESS bug: pm3_exec decoded the pm3 client's stdout as UTF-8 strictly, `hf 15 rdbl` prints an ASCII rendering of the block it read, and these two blocks hold a byte that is not valid UTF-8 (0xE1). The decode raised, the exception was caught and recorded as a failed read, and three sessions went looking for an RF cause. THE TELL WAS IN THE CAPTURED OUTPUT THE WHOLE TIME: every failure named the same byte offset -- 472 for block 0, 474 for block 1, identical across all 6 retries and all 3 sessions -- and RF flakiness does not fail deterministically to the byte. Fixed by decoding with errors='replace'; the hex column the parser actually uses is ASCII and survives intact. CONSEQUENCE FOR THIS RECORD: this tag is NOT blank. Blocks 0 and 1 hold data, and 'none found, [0,1] unread' is a record of the tool failing rather than of the card. Its `original` baseline is therefore incomplete -- and `original` is WRITE-ONCE, so a re-run will not replace it. Decide deliberately before re-baselining. Its three siblings read all 28 blocks because they are genuinely blank, so all-zero ASCII columns decoded fine -- which is why only this tag showed it.

address_space.aliasing: addr & 0x7F -- blocks 128-255 ARE blocks 0-127, one cell reachable by two addresses
address_space.evidence: A read of all 256 addresses. Each candidate PERIOD p was tested by asking whether block b holds what block b+p holds, for every b. Of the 128 candidates, exactly one gets no pair wrong: p=128. Every p from 1 to 127 fails at least one pair -- a period of 100, for instance, would need block 16 (36 F1 CD 01) to match block 116 (00 00 00 00). Seven of the agreeing pairs carry distinctive values rather than zeros -- the four factory blocks at 16/17/20/21 and the three markers written at 77/80/100 -- so the result is not zeros matching zeros.
address_space.still_open: Whether all 128 are physical storage. Blocks 80 and 100 take writes and hold them, so at least 101 addresses are real cells; 101-127 read as zero and have never been written to.
address_space.withdraws: 'it answers a read at EVERY address in the 8-bit block space, all 256, so no read-based probe can find its edge' (2026-09-08). True as stated and misleading: the top half is a mirror, not memory. The edge IS findable -- it is at 128 -- but only by comparing contents across addresses, which no probe here did. The earlier '82 phys' figure was the probe's own search ceiling and is also withdrawn.

write_side_confirmation.test: Both 100 and 228 read 00 00 00 00. Wrote FE ED BE EF to 228; 228 AND 100 both read it back. Wrote 00 00 00 00 to 228; both read zero again.
write_side_confirmation.why_it_matters: The read sweep could not tell an ALIAS from a shadow -- a card that duplicates its contents into a second region would produce identical reads at b and b+128 and is a different thing. Writing through the HIGH address and seeing the LOW one change rules that out: there is one cell and two ways to name it. It also means the high half is not read-only, so a write up there is a write to real memory rather than a discarded one.

white-card.note:
Arrived in a separate shipment from the 2026-09-08 batch and probed 2026-09-13. Ships BLANK WITH A ZERO UID -- 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00, returned in the UID field of GET SYSTEM INFO across three separate captures, so it is the card's answer and not a failed read. sysinfo 00 0F 00*10 1B 03 01 = 28 blocks x 4 bytes, IC ref 0x01, DSFID/AFI zero.

The zero UID is the only discriminator available. Geometry does not separate the candidates: white-tag-1/2/3 are also IC ref 0x01 at 28x4 and white-tag-1 measured NON-magic, while the three slix-1k gen1 cards are also IC ref 0x01 at 28x4. What differs is that every one of those carries a laser-programmed UID beginning 0xE0 plus a manufacturer byte. A UID of all zeros means the UID lives in writable storage and was never programmed, i.e. a magic card that has not been given an identity.

gen2 is excluded more firmly than the run reported. proxmark's `csetuid --v2` writes its own default CFG (64x4, IC ref 0x8B) as a side effect, and the post-attempt sysinfo is byte-identical at 1B 03 01 -- so the card ignored the custom 0xE0 frames outright rather than taking CFG and refusing the UID. No geometry was moved and there is nothing to restore.

NOT ARMED, deliberately, and it is the only card in the inventory that is not. All five gen1 cards carry gen1_write true, which only the full four-frame sequence sets, and nothing clears that register (#255) -- so every gen1 test the app has ever run went against a card that was already unlocked, where the UID moves on a write to 56/57 regardless of whether the app's own unlock/commit frames do anything. On the armed lri2k-keychain those two frames are REFUSED with error 0x10 and the UID still moves. This card is the only instrument that can test the app's own unlock sequence, and the test is one-shot: unlocking is intrinsic to setting a gen1 UID, so whoever writes first spends it. Spend it on the Flipper (gen1 clone from a 28-block source), not on the probe. What it CANNOT answer, despite being the obvious use: whether a wipe moves a virgin gen1 card's UID -- the UID starts at zeros, so a wipe that moved it to zeros is invisible.

expected.note: 64 x 4 = 256 bytes = 2048 bits; the three figures agree. UID-changeable means magic; gen2 is the expectation, but the listing does not say which generation.

white-coin.note: Confirmed gen2 magic on hardware 2026-08-24 -- gen2 UID write took and read back, so the destructive gen1 probe never ran and no data block was touched. expected.note: THE LISTING'S BIT FIGURE IS TOTAL SILICON, NOT USER MEMORY. 1024 bits = 128 bytes = 32 blocks, but an ICODE SLI/SLIX addresses 28 of them as user blocks (28 x 4 = 112 bytes = 896 bits); the remaining 4 blocks are the system/config area. So expect 28, not 32. Reporting 32 would mean the listing quoted USER memory and this is a different part. IC ref 0x01 is the SLI/SLIX family. Expected non-magic.
